items.title: Generalized Jucys-Murphy primary idempotents and the residue-summand functors $E_i$, $F_i$
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

**(ii) Content sums and blocks.** The symmetric group $S_n$ permutes the
coordinates of sequences, and two sequences are called *equivalent* when they
differ by a permutation, i.e. when they have the same content (the same
multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). For a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ put $I_\alpha:=\{\mathbf i:
\mathbf i\text{ is a permutation of }\alpha\}$ and
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 11), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves the centrality, idempotency and orthogonality of the sums
$e_\alpha$ and then uses only those properties; primitivity and
exhaustiveness are recorded from the cited block theorem, not re-proved here.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i,\alpha}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$ put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.
items.strategy: A definition item with its construction proof. Form the commutative algebra $B=k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$. Since $k$ has characteristic $p$, every eigenvalue of every $L_r$ on the regular module lies in the prime field $\mathbb F_p$ (Kleshchev survey, Lemma 2.4, printed p. 8), so the minimal polynomials split into powers of the linear factors $X-a$, $a\in\mathbb F_p$; iterated Bezout/Chinese-remainder projection for the commuting generators ([[thm-chinese-remainder-theorem-for-comaximal-ideals]]) produces the primary idempotents $P_{r,a}$ and their products $e(\mathbf i)$. The scaffold clause that every $e(\mathbf i)$ commutes with $S_{n-1}$ is false (the corrected item proves this by exact computation); the $S_{n-1}$-stable objects carrying the residue decomposition are the content sums $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}$ and the functor idempotents $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(n-1)}P_{n,i}$, and the functors $E_i,F_i$ are defined and proved stable through these. The identification of the content sums with the block idempotents is the recorded block theorem (Kleshchev survey §2.9, equation (2.41), printed p. 11); the residue-summand functors are the level-one specialization of (7.16)-(7.17) and Lemma 7.1 of the same source (printed pp. 30-31). Centrality, idempotency, orthogonality, exactness, additivity, finite-dimensionality preservation and duality compatibility are proved locally. Sources: Kleshchev survey §§2.3-2.4, (2.6)-(2.8), §2.9 (2.41), §7.4 (7.16)-(7.17), Lemma 7.1 (printed pp. 8-11, 30-31). No algebraic closedness, splitting, or choice hypothesis is used.

items.title: Residue signatures, normal, good, conormal and cogood nodes
items.statement:
Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence a terminal word is
$+^a0^c-^b$ for some $a,b,c\ge0$. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. A
terminating and locally confluent rewriting relation is confluent, so the
terminal word is unique; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has no $i$-nodes and empty signature, with
$\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for all $i$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
items.strategy: A definition item fixing the residue, ordering, cancellation and naming conventions used by the whole page. It is the level-one, zero-charge specialization of Kleshchev's signature of a node of a multipartition (Kleshchev, *Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups and Related Hecke Algebras*, §§3.4, complete 66-page arXiv:0909.4844, printed pp. 18-19: nodes ordered so that $A_m$ is above $A_{m+1}$, residues $k_m+(b-a)$, cancellation of $-+$ pairs), together with §11.4 (printed p. 53: normal $\leftrightarrow$ surviving $-$, conormal $\leftrightarrow$ surviving $+$, good = top normal, cogood = bottom conormal, $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ the counts). The residue sign is checked against Brundan, *Modular branching rules and the Mullineux map*, §2.2-2.4 (complete 34-page author manuscript, pp. 3-4): his $\ell$-residue is $r-c$, and by his Remark 2.4(II) his normal rows of $\lambda$ are exactly the transposed normal nodes of $\lambda'$ in Kleshchev's convention. No choice principle is used and no module theory is invoked; the existence and uniqueness of the reduced word follow from the cancellation procedure.

items.title: Finite-group induction is coinduction, hence biadjoint to restriction
items.statement:
Let $H\le G$ be finite groups and let $k$ be any field. For every left
$kH$-module $M$ the map
$$\Phi_M:\ \operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=kG\otimes_{kH}M\longrightarrow\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{kH}(kG,M),\qquad \Phi_M(g\otimes m)(x)=\begin{cases}(xg)m,&xg\in H,\\ 0,&xg\notin H,\end{cases}$$
is a natural isomorphism of $kG$-modules
([[def-restriction-induction-and-coinduction-for-group-modules]]). Consequently
$\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\cong\operatorname{Coind}_H^G$ naturally, so induction
is both a left and a right adjoint of restriction
([[thm-induction-is-left-adjoint-and-coinduction-right-adjoint-to-restriction]])
and is exact. No hypothesis on the characteristic of $k$, on splitting
fields, or on the prime $2$ is needed, and the argument is choice-free: it
uses only the finite selection of least representatives of the finitely many
left cosets.
items.strategy: Define $\Phi_M$ as displayed. It is $kH$-linear in $x$: $(x h)g=hg$... precisely, $\Phi_M(g\otimes hm)(x)=(xg)(hm)=((xg)h)m=\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(xh)$ for $h\in H$, so it respects the balancing relation; and $\Phi_M(g_0g\otimes m)(x)=(xg_0g)m=\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(xg_0)$, so it is a $kG$-map. Fix a left-coset transversal $R$ of $H$ in $G$ and send a coinduced map $\varphi$ to $\sum_{r\in R}r^{-1}\otimes\varphi(r)$; the two constructions are inverse because every $x\in G$ lies in exactly one double coset $H r$, so each summand of the inverse is supported on a single coset and the finiteness of $G/H$ makes the sums finite. Combining with the two published adjunctions gives that $\operatorname{Ind}$ is both left and right adjoint to $\operatorname{Res}$; exactness follows from $\operatorname{Ind}=\operatorname{Coind}$ together with the right-exactness of induction, or alternatively from the freeness of $kG$ over $kH$ ([[lem-the-group-ring-is-free-over-a-subgroup-ring]]). This is the exact finite-group relative Frobenius isomorphism used for the modular biadjunction of the branching page; the argument uses the fixed transversal $R$ and is choice-free in the finite setting.

items.title: The socle of an uncoloured modular restriction is the multiplicity-free sum over the good residues
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted
partition of $d\ge1$; write $D(\mu)$ for the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).
Let $A_i$ denote the good $i$-node of $\mu$, for those
$i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Then
$$\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}\bigl(D(\mu){\downarrow}_{S_{d-1}}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{i:\,\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0}D(\mu\setminus A_i),$$
a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules: distinct residues give
distinct summands. The sum runs over the residues $i$ with
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, one good node per such residue; the completely
reducible special case (the restriction is semisimple if and only if every
normal node is good, Kleshchev II Theorem 0.6) is a separate statement and is
not asserted here.
items.strategy: The source theorem is Kleshchev II (1995) Theorem 0.5 (socle $=$ sum over good nodes, with equal head), restated as Kleshchev survey Theorem 11.6/§11.4 (printed pp. 53-54); a complete proof-bearing version in this page's convention is Brundan 1998 Theorems 2.6 and 5.4 together with the Schur-functor deduction in Brundan §5.5-5.7 (the socle of $L_n(\lambda)^1|_{U(n-1)}$ is $\bigoplus_{i\in R^{good}(\lambda)}L_{n-1}(\lambda(i))$), translated by Brundan Remark 2.4(II) (normal/good nodes of $\lambda$ are the transposed normal/good nodes of $\lambda'$). The residue decomposition refines the displayed socle through $\operatorname{Res}=\bigoplus_iE_i$ ([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]): the good $i$-node contributes to the $i$-summand, and the good nodes of distinct residues lie in distinct summands, so the sum is multiplicity-free. The completely-reducible case is Kleshchev II Theorem 0.6; it is recorded only as the special case it is, not as the general restriction. Choice-free. The refinement used on the companion page (two good nodes force decomposability) is Remark 2.7 of Brundan 1998: the good-node socle summands lie in pairwise different blocks of $H(r-1)$, hence occupy different block components of the restriction; that remark is cited rather than restated as a separate item.

items.title: Good-node deletion and cogood-node addition operators
items.statement:
On the set of $p$-restricted partitions
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]) define partial operators
$\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ for $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ by
$$\tilde e_i\mu:=\mu\setminus A\quad\text{if }\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $A$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]), the
operator being undefined on $\mu$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; and
$$\tilde f_i\mu:=\mu\cup B\quad\text{if }\varphi_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $B$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$, the operator being undefined on
$\mu$ when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. Then
$$\mu=\tilde f_i\nu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$$
for all $p$-restricted $\mu,\nu$; in particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$
are mutual inverses on their domains, each $\tilde e_i$ lowers the rank by one
and each $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one, and at most one good and at most
one cogood node exist in each residue. No module-theoretic statement is made
here: this item is pure combinatorics, and the identification of these
operators with the crystal operators of the level-one Fock space is a theorem
of the later Fock-space page, not an input here.
items.strategy: A combinatorial definition item whose mutual-inverse property and closure are proved locally rather than cited. The proof runs the stack algorithm for the reduced signature: cancellation leaves a word $+^a0^c-^b$, and the flip lemma identifies the first surviving $-$ with the last surviving $+$ of the shifted word, so a removable node $A$ is good for $\mu$ if and only if it is cogood for $\mu\setminus A$; the geometric comparison of the $i$-words of $\mu$ and $\mu\setminus X$ then gives the iff property for the operators, and the two bad-case analyses show that both operators stay inside the $p$-restricted partitions. The scaffold fact asserting general preservation of removable nodes was false and is replaced by this argument. The identification of these operators with the crystal operators of the level-one Fock space is deliberately not asserted here (Kleshchev survey §3.4, printed p. 19; combinatorics only).

items.title: Every $p$-restricted partition is reached from the empty partition by cogood additions
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$. Every $p$-restricted partition
$\mu$ of $d$ is obtained from the empty partition by $d$ successive cogood
additions: there are residues $i_1,\dots,i_d$ with
$$\mu=\tilde f_{i_d}\cdots\tilde f_{i_1}\varnothing;$$
equivalently, every $p$-restricted $\mu\ne\varnothing$ has at least one good
node, and successive good deletions carry $\mu$ to $\varnothing$
([[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]],
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Hence, in
the graph whose vertices are the $p$-restricted partitions and whose edges
join $\nu$ to $\tilde f_i\nu$ for every $i$ for which the operator is
defined, the empty partition is the unique vertex of rank $0$ and every
vertex is reached from it; dually every vertex reaches the empty partition by
successive good deletions. The argument is choice-free.

items.title: The crystal identification does not elementarily identify the cellular simple labels
items.statement:
Two labellings of the simple modules of the group algebra $kS_d$ and of the
Hecke algebra $H_d$ are in play on this page and on the Fock-space page.

- The **cellular labels** $D(\mu)=\operatorname{hd}(S(\mu))$ are the heads of
  the Specht modules in the dual-Specht convention; they are the labels used
  by the modular classification
  ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).
- The **inductive (crystal) labels** $\dot D(\mu)$ are defined recursively
  from the residue-summand functors $F_i$ of
  [[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]] by
  $\dot D(\varnothing)=k$ and, for $\mu\ne\varnothing$,
$$\dot D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(F_i\dot D(\tilde e_i\mu)\bigr) \quad\text{for any }i\text{ with }\tilde e_i\mu\ne\varnothing,$$ the
  operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ being those of
  [[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]] and the independence
  of the choice of $i$ a theorem of the crystal theory. The two labellings
  agree, $$\dot D(\mu)\cong D(\mu)\qquad(\mu\ \text{p-restricted}),$$ and this
  identification (11.1) of Kleshchev's survey is *not* elementary: it was
  first established by Ariki and later by graded arguments, both depending on
  the full theory of the cyclotomic Hecke/KLR categorification.

Consequently no proof on this page or on the later Fock-space page may use
Fock-space reachability to establish the cellular classification of simple
modules, or the cellular classification to establish the Fock-space
component; the two directions are separated by this reminder. In particular
the socle theorem
`cor-socle-of-uncoloured-modular-restriction-is-the-sum-over-good-residues`
and the branching theorems of this page are stated and used for the cellular
labels, while any statement about the crystal operators as operators on Fock
space is a separate obligation of the Fock-space page.
items.strategy: No proof section: this is a boundary remark recorded so that neither direction of the labelling comparison is used circularly on this page or on the later Fock-space page. Provenance literature-derived (Kleshchev survey §11.2, equation (11.1), printed p. 52; the identification is due to Ariki and to the graded arguments cited there).

items.title: The Schur functor compares first-level branching with Hecke restriction
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell=e(F,q)$, and $n\ge r\ge1$; at the empty lower-rank boundary put $S(0,0)=H(0)=F$ with its identity functor. Use the left-module version of the q-Schur algebra $S(n,r)$ and its exact Schur functor $f_{n,r}:V\mapsto eV$ with left adjoint $h_{n,r}:X\mapsto S(n,r)e\otimes_{eS(n,r)e}X$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Right-module suppliers are converted to left modules through their star anti-involutions. All Specht and simple labels below are **Murphy labels**: $f(W^\mu)=S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $f(L_n(\mu))=D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, the latter nonzero exactly when $\mu$ is $\ell$-restricted ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

For a degree-$r$ polynomial module $V=\bigoplus_{|\alpha|=r}V_\alpha$, its **first level** is $$V^1:=\bigoplus_{\alpha_n=1}V_\alpha.$$ It is a module for the Levi polynomial algebra $S(n-1,r-1)$: the first $n-1$ coordinates sum to $r-1$. It is not the sum of the weights one simple root below the highest weight. For an $\ell$-restricted partition $\lambda\vdash r$, the following hold.

1. There is a natural $H(r-1)$-module isomorphism $$f_{n-1,r-1}(L_n(\lambda)^1)\cong      \operatorname{Res}_{H(r-1)}^{H(r)}f_{n,r}(L_n(\lambda)).$$ 2. For any $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$, the Schur functor induces $$\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong      \operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV).$$ Here $W^{(e)}=S(n,r)eW$ is the intersection of submodules whose quotient is killed by $e$, and $V_{(e)}$ is the sum of submodules killed by $e$. 3. The socle of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ as a Levi module has only $\ell$-restricted labels.

For every partition $\mu\vdash r-1$ with $\mu$ $\ell$-restricted, $$[L_n(\lambda)^1:L_{n-1}(\mu)]  =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}].$$ The exact functor transfers these surviving multiplicities; it may kill nonrestricted simple factors. At $q=1$ these statements hold over every field for the group algebras. In ordinary James labels the dictionary is $D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, not an untwisted identification with $D^\lambda$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell=e(F,q)$, and $n\ge r\ge1$; at the empty lower-rank boundary put $S(0,0)=H(0)=F$ with its identity functor. Use the left-module version of the q-Schur algebra $S(n,r)$ and its exact Schur functor $f_{n,r}:V\mapsto eV$ with left adjoint $h_{n,r}:X\mapsto S(n,r)e\otimes_{eS(n,r)e}X$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Right-module suppliers are converted to left modules through their star anti-involutions. All Specht and simple labels below are **Murphy labels**: $f(W^\mu)=S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $f(L_n(\mu))=D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, the latter nonzero exactly when $\mu$ is $\ell$-restricted ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

For a degree-$r$ polynomial module $V=\bigoplus_{|\alpha|=r}V_\alpha$, its **first level** is $$V^1:=\bigoplus_{\alpha_n=1}V_\alpha.$$ It is a module for the Levi polynomial algebra $S(n-1,r-1)$: the first $n-1$ coordinates sum to $r-1$. It is not the sum of the weights one simple root below the highest weight. For an $\ell$-restricted partition $\lambda\vdash r$, the following hold.

1. There is a natural $H(r-1)$-module isomorphism $$f_{n-1,r-1}(L_n(\lambda)^1)\cong      \operatorname{Res}_{H(r-1)}^{H(r)}f_{n,r}(L_n(\lambda)).$$ 2. For any $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$, the Schur functor induces $$\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong      \operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV).$$ Here $W^{(e)}=S(n,r)eW$ is the intersection of submodules whose quotient is killed by $e$, and $V_{(e)}$ is the sum of submodules killed by $e$. 3. The socle of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ as a Levi module has only $\ell$-restricted labels.

For every partition $\mu\vdash r-1$ with $\mu$ $\ell$-restricted, $$[L_n(\lambda)^1:L_{n-1}(\mu)]  =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}].$$ The exact functor transfers these surviving multiplicities; it may kill nonrestricted simple factors. At $q=1$ these statements hold over every field for the group algebras. In ordinary James labels the dictionary is $D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, not an untwisted identification with $D^\lambda$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, ranks, polynomial weight decomposition, and q-Schur and Hecke algebras of the Statement.

[F1] The permutation-summand realization is $S(n,r)=\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(\bigoplus_\alpha M^\alpha)$, with weight projections $1_\alpha$. The regular summand for a composition with exactly $r$ entries equal to $1$ is $M^\alpha=H(r)$. The standard corner is $\omega=(1^r,0^{n-r})$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The exact Schur functor sends $W^\mu$ to $S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $L_n(\mu)$ to $D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, allowing zero images. The nonzero images have restricted labels and are pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F3] Brundan, full author manuscript, §3.22 defines polynomial levels by last-coordinate weight, using both $K_n$ and its binomial operators so the integer weight is determined even at a root of unity. The Levi $U(n-1)$ commutes with these operators. The q-Schur polynomial realization is the corresponding finite-degree quotient. In §5.5 the functors are left-module functors; star converts the right-module suppliers to this convention.

[F4] Brundan's Theorem 5.4 identifies the Levi socle of the first level with $\bigoplus_{i\in R^{\mathrm{good}}(\lambda)}L_{n-1}(\lambda(i))$; Lemma 5.7 proves these labels restricted when $\lambda$ is restricted. These are the source's intrinsic good-node labels, not an identification of cellular and crystal labels. This input is used only for assertion 3. Its full relevant proof (§5.3-5.7, printed pp. 29-32) was consulted; a new local construction of all lowering-operator theory in the preceding sections is not claimed.

[F5] At $q=1$ the actual ordinary polytabloid/signed-conjugate Murphy comparison gives the group module dictionary, with form factor $1$, over every field. It follows through the corrected Definition and the actual NEW50 comparison and specialization suppliers, not the printed-page-25 untwisted warning ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Construct the lower-rank action directly over the given field. Put $M_0=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(n-1,r-1)}M^\alpha$ for $H(r-1)$. Length-additive parabolic coset bases give $M^{(\alpha,1)}\cong M^\alpha\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ by $x_\alpha h\otimes a\mapsto x_\alpha ha$. Thus the summands with last coordinate $1$ form $M_1\cong M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$. The functorial algebra homomorphism $f\mapsto f\otimes1$ embeds $S(n-1,r-1)$ into $\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(M_1)$: the Hecke algebra $H(r)$ is free on its parabolic coset basis and contains the unit coset, so the map is injective. Extend these maps by zero to the remaining summands of $M$ and put $p=\sum_{\alpha_n=1}1_\alpha$. For every left $S(n,r)$-module $V$, $V^1=pV$ is therefore a natural $S(n-1,r-1)$-module. This supplies the lower-rank action without assuming that the first level is a sum of root-adjacent highest-weight spaces, and without adjoining a square root of the Hecke parameter. It agrees with the last-coordinate polynomial level of [F3]. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Prove the Hom assertion algebraically. For $S=S(n,r)$ put $\overline W=Se\otimes_{eSe}eW$ and let $\varepsilon:\overline W\to W$ send $se\otimes w$ to $sw$. Its image is $SeW=W^{(e)}$, which is $W$ under the stated hypothesis. Applying $e$ identifies $e\varepsilon$ with the isomorphism $eSe\otimes_{eSe}eW\to eW$. Exactness of $e(-)$ therefore gives $eK=0$ for $K=\ker\varepsilon$. The exact sequence is $$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\overline W   \xrightarrow{\varepsilon}W\longrightarrow0.$$ For any $S$-map $g:\overline W\to V$, its image $g(K)$ is an $S$-submodule killed by $e$, so it is contained in $V_{(e)}=0$. Thus $g$ factors uniquely through $W$. The adjunction then gives $\operatorname{Hom}_H(eW,eV)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(\overline W,V) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(W,V)$. This proves assertion 2, with the kernel and quotient in the correct direction. [given, F1]

2.1 Reconcile the corners for all $n\ge r$. Put $\omega_*=(1^{r-1},0^{n-r},1)$ and $e_*=1_{\omega_*}$. Both $M^\omega$ and $M^{\omega_*}$ are the regular module $H(r)$. Their fixed identity isomorphism gives block matrix units $u,v\in S(n,r)$ with $u=e_*ue$, $v=eve_*$, $uv=e_*$ and $vu=e$. Thus multiplication by $u$ gives a natural isomorphism $eV\to e_*V$, with inverse multiplication by $v$, and carries the standard regular corner action to the $e_*$ corner action. When $n=r$ these corners coincide. This explicitly supplies the natural corner identification instead of treating an idempotent with last coordinate $0$ as lying in the first level. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 The restricted-socle assertion is Brundan's Lemma 5.7. By [F4] every socle label is $\lambda(i)$ for a good row $i$. If it were not restricted while $\lambda$ is restricted, then $i>1$ and $\lambda_{i-1}-\lambda_i=\ell-1$. The last nodes of rows $i-1$ and $i$ then have equal residue, and the source's normality criterion forces row $i-1$ to be normal, contradicting the minimality of the good row $i$ in that residue. Thus all socle labels are restricted. At $\ell=\infty$ all partitions are restricted. For the stable-rank boundary $n=r$ with $\lambda_n>0$, necessarily $\lambda=(1^r)$: the determinant module and its first level are one-dimensional determinant modules, and the conclusion holds directly. [F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Compute the first-level corner inside this induced action. The lower regular summand is $H(r-1)$, whose induction is $H(r-1)\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)=H(r)$, exactly the summand of type $\omega_*$. Its weight projection on $pV$ is $e_*$, so $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)=e_*V$. The lower corner operator given by left multiplication by $h\in H(r-1)$ induces left multiplication by the same $h$ on $H(r)$ under $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. Thus every generator $T_1,\ldots,T_{r-2}$ acts exactly as its image in the upper regular corner, by equality of these explicit endomorphisms. The matrix units of step 2.1 identify the upper standard corner with this regular summand. They consequently give $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)\cong\operatorname{Res}f_{n,r}(V)$ on every module. This is an algebra-level calculation; it needs no generic semisimplicity or cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Transfer composition multiplicities by exactness, not by a Hom-space count. Apply $f_{n-1,r-1}$ to a finite composition series of $L_n(\lambda)^1$. By [F2] its factors become either zero or the pairwise nonisomorphic $D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}$ for restricted $\mu$. Removing repeated terms of the resulting filtration therefore preserves the number of each surviving simple factor. Step 3.1 identifies its result with $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}$, proving the stated equality. Assertion 3 is not used to claim that every composition factor survives; a socle statement alone would not justify that claim. [F2, step 3.1]

5.1 At $q=1$, [F5] identifies the corner algebras with group algebras. In ordinary regular labels the two modules are simultaneously twisted by sign and both partition labels are conjugated. Sign restricts along the group tower, is exact, and preserves the two compared multiplicities. This is the ordinary group interpretation, including characteristic $2$; it is not an untwisted identification of a restricted label with the same regular label. Steps 3.1, 1.2, 2.2 and 4.1 prove all the assertions. [F5, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

The first-level and ordinary-label reconciliation above is the new authored binding repair. The previously accepted source20 cell-form repair and NEW50 ordinary polytabloid construction are unchanged. Actual acceptance requires the repaired current source20/NEW50 supplier carriers after the live writers drain and the same reviewer checks the actual bound interfaces. No further primitive bridge construction is claimed. ## Statement

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ (every field is splitting for symmetric groups, so no algebraic closedness is needed) and let $\lambda$ be a $p$-regular partition of $n$ ([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]), so that $D^\lambda$ is the simple head of the Specht module $S^\lambda_k$ ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). Let $A=(j,\lambda_j)$ be a removable node of $\lambda$ whose removal $\lambda(j)$ is again $p$-regular, and call $A$ **normal** for $\lambda$ when the transposed node $(\lambda_j,j)$ of the $p$-restricted partition $\lambda'$ is a normal node in the sense of [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]] (this is Kleshchev's normality; it is computed in the reduced signature of the correct residue class of $\lambda'$). Then $$[\,D^\lambda{\downarrow}_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}\,]=0$$ if $A$ is not normal, and $$[\,D^\lambda{\downarrow}_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}\,]=1+\#\{B:\ B\ \text{is a normal removable node of }\lambda\text{ strictly above }A\text{ with }\operatorname{res}(B)=\operatorname{res}(A)\}$$ if $A$ is normal. Here $\operatorname{res}$ is the residue $c-r\bmod p$ and "above" means strictly smaller row index. Equivalently, the multiplicity is the first-level multiplicity $\gamma(A)$ of Kleshchev 1997, so it is the number of normal nodes of $\lambda$ weakly above $A$ in $A$'s residue class, and $A$ is normal precisely when this number is nonzero.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$, a $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$ and a removable node $A=(j,\lambda_j)$ with $\lambda(j)$ $p$-regular.

[F1] The residue-summand decomposition of the restriction and the dictionary between the $p$-regular and the $p$-restricted labels: $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ for $p$-restricted $\mu$, and the transposed node dictionary of Brundan Remark 2.4(II) translates normality of a removable node of $\lambda$ into normality of the transposed node of $\lambda'$ in the signature sense of [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]] ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]).

[F2] Apply the corrected Schur-functor comparison to the **restricted** partition $\mu=\lambda'$, and to $\nu=\lambda(j)'$ at the lower degree. For a stable Schur rank $N\ge n$, its first level consists of polynomial weights with last coordinate $1$. The comparison and exactness give $$[L_N(\mu)^1:L_{N-1}(\nu)]   =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\nu}].$$ At $q=1$, the actual signed-conjugate dictionary says $D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}\cong D^\lambda\otimes\operatorname{sgn}_n$ and $D_{\mathrm M}^{\nu}\cong D^{\lambda(j)}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}_{n-1}$. Since sign restricts to sign, twisting **both** modules leaves the multiplicity unchanged. This proves the precise group-to-first-level transfer used below ([[prop-schur-functor-compares-first-level-branching-with-hecke-restriction]], [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]). No Schur functor is applied to the ordinary regular label $\lambda$ as if it were restricted.

[F3] The source's algebraic-group count is indexed by dominant weights, not by the characteristic as a rank. In Kleshchev §11 take $N=n$, $l=N-1$, and let $w_n(\lambda)$ be the type-$A_l$ dominant weight whose fundamental-weight coefficients are $\lambda'_a-\lambda'_{a+1}$. It is the weight underlying the polynomial highest weight $\mu=\lambda'$. The lower label is $w_{n-1}(\lambda(j))$, and for $\lambda\ne(n)$ $$w_{n-1}(\lambda(j))=\operatorname{res}_{A_{l-1}}    \bigl(w_n(\lambda)-\alpha(\lambda_j,l)\bigr).$$ Theorem 9.3 computes the corresponding multiplicity in the first level restricted to $A_{l-1}$; §11, Proposition 11.2 and the deduction on printed pp. 64-65 identify this count with the one at the removed ordinary node. The index is the column $\lambda_j$ after conjugation, not the ordinary row $j$ treated as an unchanged Schur label. The combinatorial recurrence and basis results of Part I/II remain the recorded source inputs; their full local reconstruction is not claimed by this binding repair. For $\lambda=(n)$ the ordinary module is trivial and its sole removable-node multiplicity is $1$, handled directly. The case $n=1$ is the trivial restriction to $S_0$. Neither $A_{p-1}$ nor a rank determined by the characteristic is used.

[F4] Kleshchev 1997, Theorem 1.4 and its reformulation (manuscript p. 5), together with Corollary 5.8(ii) (manuscript p. 44) and the index identities $\lambda_k-\lambda_j+j-k+1=B_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,\lambda_k)$ and $\lambda_k-\lambda_j+j-k=C_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,\lambda_k)$ used on manuscript pp. 64-65: the corresponding root-indexed count $\gamma_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,l)$ of [F3] equals $1$ plus the number of normal nodes of $\lambda$ strictly above $A$ in the same residue class when $A$ is normal, and is $0$ when $A$ is not normal.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Reduction to the correctly labelled first level. Put $\mu=\lambda'$ and $\nu=\lambda(j)'$. These are $p$-restricted because both ordinary labels are $p$-regular. By [F2], the exact first-level comparison identifies the multiplicity of $L_{N-1}(\nu)$ in $L_N(\mu)^1$ with the multiplicity of $D_{\mathrm M}^{\nu}$ in $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}$. At $q=1$, twist both compared modules by sign, which restricts along $S_{n-1}\subset S_n$, and use the conjugate-label dictionary. This yields exactly $[D^\lambda\downarrow_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}]$. The algebraic weight and removed-root indexing are those of [F3]. In particular neither the ordinary regular label itself nor the characteristic is substituted for a Schur label or algebraic-group rank. [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 The first-level multiplicity is the combinatorial count. By the theorem recorded in [F3], the corresponding first-level multiplicity at the transposed removed node, indexed as in [F3], is the integer $\gamma_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,l)$ of the source's first-level recurrence, which is computed by the recurrence recorded in [F3]; no Fock-space or Ariki input is used. [step 1.1, F3]

3.1 Identification of the count. By the results recorded in [F4], the count $\gamma_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,l)$ is $0$ when $A$ is not normal and equals $1+\#\{B:B\text{ normal removable node of }\lambda\text{ strictly above }A,\ \operatorname{res}(B)=\operatorname{res}(A)\}$ when $A$ is normal; the two expressions of the statement both describe this integer, and the normality of $A$ is read in the reduced signature of $\lambda'$ via the transposed-node dictionary of [F1]. [step 2.1, F1, F4]

4.1 Calibration with the source's worked example. For $p=3$ and $\lambda=(5,3,2)$ the removable nodes are $(1,5)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,2)$ with residues $5-1=4\equiv1$, $3-2\equiv1$, $2-3\equiv2$; transposing gives $\lambda'=(3,3,2,1,1)$, in which the nodes $(3,2),(5,1)$ and no further node form the normal $2$-class, so the normal nodes of $\lambda$ are $(2,3)$ and $(1,5)$, and the formula gives multiplicities $2$ (for $(2,3)$, with one normal node above it) and $1$ (for $(1,5)$); the node $(3,2)$ is not normal and contributes $0$. This reproduces the multiplicities $1,2,0$ recorded in the source (manuscript p. 5) for the nodes $(1,5),(2,3),(3,2)$. [step 3.1, F1, F4]

5.1 Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 give $[D^\lambda\downarrow_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}]=0$ for non-normal $A$ and the displayed count for normal $A$, and step 4.1 checks the normalization against the source's example. The reduction of step 1.1 uses only the $q=1$ specialization of the Schur-functor comparison; the combinatorial inputs [F3] and [F4] are the recorded content of Kleshchev 1997, whose Part I/II arguments are cited by exact locators and not replaced by a weaker statement. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

items.title: Normal-node composition multiplicities under residue restriction
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $A$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$ such that $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
is again $p$-restricted; let $D(\mu)$ be the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$ in the dual-Specht (cellular) convention, so that
$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]],
[[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]), and let
$E_i$ be the residue-summand functor of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]. Then
$$[\,E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=0$$
if $A$ is not a normal $i$-node of $\mu$, and
$$[\,E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=\#\{B:\ B\ \text{normal }i\text{-node of }\mu\text{ weakly below }A\}$$
(counting $A$ itself) if $A$ is normal. The corresponding
Specht-to-restriction Hom criterion (Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5, equivalently
Kleshchev II Theorem 0.4) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.
items.strategy: Transfer the p-regular theorem [[thm-kleshchev-first-level-branching-multiplicity]] through the transpose/sign duality $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ of the published dictionary item: restriction multiplicities are unchanged by the sign twist, the transpose exchanges rows and columns so 'strictly above $A$' becomes 'weakly below $A$', and residues negate, $c-r\mapsto r-c$; at $p=2$ the sign is trivial but neither the transpose nor the order reversal may be dropped. The residue summand $E_i$ is the projection onto the summand of $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)$ whose JM content ends in $i$; since the composition factor $D(\nu)$ differs from $\mu$ by the node $A$ of residue $i$, it lies in that summand and the projection does not change its multiplicity. This is Kleshchev's Theorem 11.6(ii) (Kleshchev survey, printed pp. 53-54, attributed there to Kleshchev 1995, 1997) and it is the exact form used by the residue functors of this page. The count direction 'above $\to$ below' and the residue negation were verified against the source's worked example $p=3$, $\lambda=(5,3,2)$ with multiplicities $1,2,0$ (Kleshchev 1997 p. 5), whose transpose $\mu=(3,3,2,1,1)$ gives the normal $2$-nodes $(3,2),(5,1)$ and the counts $2$ and $1$.

criterion (Kleshchev survey Theorem 11.7(i), Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5 dual
form) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.

items.title: The good node gives the simple socle and head of the residue restriction
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$; let $A$ be the good
$i$-node and $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). For the
residue-summand functor $E_i$ of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]] the
module $E_iD(\mu)$ has simple socle and simple head, both isomorphic to
$D(\nu)$, and the total (ungraded) multiplicity of $D(\nu)$ in $E_iD(\mu)$ is
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)$. Thus the Loewy endpoints are simple even though the
formal character of $E_iD(\mu)$ may contain the additional normal-node

items.strategy: Socle: by ([[cor-socle-of-uncoloured-modular-restriction-is-the-sum-over-good-residues]]) the socle of $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)$ is $\bigoplus_{j:\varepsilon_j>0}D(\mu\setminus A_j)$, a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules; the $i$-summand $E_iD(\mu)$ contains precisely the summand $D(\mu\setminus A)=D(\nu)$ (the good $i$-node is unique for its residue). Head: the contragredient dual of $E_iD(\mu)$ is $E_i(D(\mu)^*)\cong E_iD(\mu)$ because the primary idempotents are invariant under the antipode ([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]) and $D(\mu)$ is self-dual; for a finite-dimensional self-dual module the head is the dual of the socle, so the head is $D(\nu)$ as well ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Multiplicity: apply the normal-node theorem ([[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]]) with $A$ the good node; the normal $i$-nodes weakly below $A$ are exactly all normal $i$-nodes, whose number is $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$. The ungraded statement is the one asserted; no graded shift is displayed before the Hecke/KLR bridge. Source: Kleshchev survey Theorem 11.6(ii) with the socle statement of §11.4; the complete proof in the Hecke convention is Brundan 1998 Theorems 5.4 and the §5.5-5.7 transfer, valid at $p=2$.

items.title: The cogood node gives the simple socle and head of the residue induction
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varphi_i(\mu)>0$; let $B$ be the cogood
$i$-node and $\nu=\mu\cup B$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Then
$F_iD(\mu)$ has simple socle and simple head, both isomorphic to $D(\nu)$,
and the total (ungraded) multiplicity of $D(\nu)$ in $F_iD(\mu)$ is
$\varphi_i(\mu)$
([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]).
items.strategy: The proof uses the recorded dual source statement (Kleshchev survey §11.4 with Theorem 11.7; Brundan §5.5) for the simple socle and head, and computes the total multiplicity $\varphi_i(\mu)$ locally from the conormal-node theorem applied to the cogood node $B$, which is the bottommost conormal node. The endpoint identification is completed by antipode-invariance of the residue idempotents and self-duality of the simple modules (head = dual of socle), and the characteristic-$2$ calibration $p=2$, $\mu=(1)$ checks $F_1D(1)\cong kS_2$ with socle, head and total multiplicity $2$ $= \varphi_1(1)$. The proof does not use any unshifted duality of $F_i$ and $E_i$.

title: Modular Branching and the Good-Node Crystal — Examples

items.title: A full cogood-addition path from the empty partition to (3,1,1) at p = 3
items.statement:
At $p=3$ the $p$-restricted partition $(3,1,1)$ is reached from the empty
partition by the five cogood additions
$$\varnothing\xrightarrow{\,0\,}(1)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}(1,1)\xrightarrow{\,1\,}(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,1\,}(2,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}(3,1,1),$$
that is, $(1)=\tilde f_0\varnothing$, $(1,1)=\tilde f_2(1)$,
$(1,1,1)=\tilde f_1(1,1)$, $(2,1,1)=\tilde f_1(1,1,1)$,
$(3,1,1)=\tilde f_2(2,1,1)$, where the labels record the residues of the
added nodes
([[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]]). Reversing the path
gives the good deletions
$$(3,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}(2,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,1\,}(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,1\,}(1,1)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}(1)\xrightarrow{\,0\,}\varnothing.$$
The relevant reduced signatures are: $(1)$ at $i=0$: $(-)$; $(1,1)$ at
$i=2$: $(-)$; $(1,1,1)$ at $i=1$: $(+,-)$; $(2,1,1)$ at $i=1$: $(-,-)$;
$(3,1,1)$ at $i=2$: $(-)$; and $(1,1)$ at $i=1$: $(+,+)$,
$(2,1,1)$ at $i=2$: $(+)$. This is a case in which the reduced signatures are
not multiplicity-free: the signature $(+,-)$ occurs at $i=1$ for $(1,1,1)$.
items.strategy: Direct computation from the signature definition: list the addable and removable nodes of each partition (for $(1)$: removable $(1,1)$ at residue $0$; for $(1,1)$: removable $(2,1)$ at residue $2$, addables $(1,2),(3,1)$ at residue $1$; for $(1,1,1)$: removable $(3,1)$ at residue $1$, addables $(1,2)$ at residue $1$ and $(4,1)$ at residue $0$; for $(2,1,1)$: removable $(1,2),(3,1)$ at residue $1$, addables $(1,3)$ at residue $2$, $(2,2)$ and $(4,1)$ at residue $0$; for $(3,1,1)$: removable $(1,3)$ at residue $2$, addables $(1,4),(2,2),(4,1)$ at residue $0$), cancel $-+$ pairs top to bottom, and read off the rightmost $+$ (cogood) and the leftmost $-$ (good) of each residue. Every forward step is the addition of a cogood node and every reverse step the deletion of a good node, as predicted by the mutual-inverse property of the crystal operators; the path also verifies the reachability proposition in a case where the reduced signatures are not multiplicity-free. Method: Kleshchev survey §3.4 (printed pp. 18-19).

items.title: Normal and good nodes for the partition (6,4,4,3,2)
items.statement:
Work Brundan's Example 2.8 (complete 34-page author manuscript, p. 5) in his
conventions: $\lambda=(6,4,4,3,2)$ is $\ell$-restricted for $\ell=3$ and
$\ell=4$, residues are $r-c\bmod\ell$ in the source's orientation (the
negative of the $c-r$ convention of this page,
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]),
$R(\lambda)=\{1,3,4,5\}$ is the set of removable rows, and for
$i\in R(\lambda)$ one compares $B_{i,5}(\lambda)\cap R(\lambda)$ with
$C_{i,5}(\lambda)\cap R(\lambda)$ in the lattice order $\downarrow$, where
$$B_{i,j}(\lambda)=\{k\in[i..j):\operatorname{res}_\ell(i,\lambda_i)= \operatorname{res}_\ell(k+1,\lambda_{k+1}+1)\},\qquad C_{i,j}(\lambda)=\{k\in(i..j):\operatorname{res}_\ell(i,\lambda_i)= \operatorname{res}_\ell(k,\lambda_k)\},$$
and $A\downarrow B$ means that there is an injection $\theta:A\to B$ with
$\theta(a)\le a$ for all $a$.

For $\ell=3$ the removable nodes have residues $1,2,1,0$ for
$i=1,3,4,5$ and
$$(B\cap R,C\cap R)=(\varnothing,\{4\}),\ (\{4\},\varnothing), (\varnothing,\varnothing),\ (\varnothing,\varnothing);$$
hence $R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,4,5\}$ and, since rows $4$ and $1$ share
residue $1$, $R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1,5\}$. For $\ell=4$ the residues are
$3,3,1,3$ and
$$(B\cap R,C\cap R)=(\varnothing,\{3,5\}),\ (\varnothing,\{5\}), (\varnothing,\varnothing),\ (\varnothing,\varnothing);$$
hence row $4$ is normal-refuted by $\{5\}\not\downarrow\varnothing$ and
$R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,3,5\}$, and since rows $1,3,5$ share residue $3$,
$R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1\}$. By the branching theorems the restriction of
$D^{\lambda}$ to $H(r-1)$ is therefore decomposable for $\ell=3$ (socle
$D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}\oplus D^{(6,4,4,3,1)}$) and indecomposable for $\ell=4$
(socle $D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}$).
items.strategy: A finite verification of Brundan's Example 2.8 (pp. 4-5), carried out in the source's transposed convention and translated back to the $c-r$ dictionary of the page: the removable rows, residues and the index sets $B_{i,j},C_{i,j}$ are recomputed row by row for $\ell=3$ and $\ell=4$, the lattice tests $A\downarrow B$ give $R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,4,5\}$, $R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1,5\}$ at $\ell=3$ and $R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,3,5\}$, $R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1\}$ at $\ell=4$, and the branching theorems then give decomposability at $\ell=3$ (socle $D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}\oplus D^{(6,4,4,3,1)}$) and indecomposability at $\ell=4$ with the corrected simple socle $D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}=D^{\lambda(1)}$ (the scaffold's label $D^{(6,4,4,2,2)}$ and its loose (2.9) citation are wrong and are repaired here; Brundan Theorem 2.6 with §2.10 supplies the socle). The example shows that the residue list alone does not determine normality and that good nodes are the minimal normal nodes per residue.
